surfaces.part: forest canopy tile block (repeating leaf clumps)

answer.evidence: The object is a tiled autotile sample of dense foliage: a roughly 96px wide block with a bump at the top, filled with a repeating pattern of leaf clumps. Column scans show a repeating period of 16 rows (e.g. x=64: 3/5/8 rows of light, mid, dark repeating) with no front-edge line, no eave shadow, no ellipse, and no distinct front face. The width profile is constant (about 95) from row 20 to 79, so there is no widening and narrowing that would indicate a cap. It reads as a flat top-down texture, not a standing 3/4 object.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a canopy autotile block with scalloped clumps in dark greens plus a few lighter leaf-cluster dots. Its outline is a dark green tint, not black (0% neutral edge pixels, matching the references), and it has no 5x5 flat fills. It is far below the references on the measured facts: 14 distinct colours against 427 and 567, and 12 colours per tile against about 108. By eye it has roughly 4 green steps against 5-6 in the references, and the highlights are sparse and muted. Leaf clumps are small and uniform, with no bright lit top edge, so the mass reads flat and low-contrast next to the bright, layered canopies of the references. The reference trees are also whole trees with trunks, so some of the gap comes from the piece type, but the shading depth is still clearly shallower. Density is much lower, so it fails.

answer.evidence: The object is a tiled autotile sample of repeating leaf clumps. The silhouette is a wide block (width about 96) with a narrower bump at rows 0-16 (width about 30). No flat fills (0% coverage), but the canopy is shallower and flatter than the references. Autotile tiles may legitimately be simpler, yet the gap in colours and in highlight/shade range is too large to accept it next to the references.
